name: Orbital rubbing / eye socket massage

lead: Orbital rubbing is a bonehack in which people press or massage the area around the eye socket, aiming for a more open, defined eye area and a change in how the orbit looks. It is discussed as a non-surgical option for eye-area aesthetics.

The idea is that sustained manual pressure remodels bone around the socket. The orbit is a rigid cavity formed by seven bones, and no clinical study has tested whether massage changes it; community material on the practice is sparse.

paras: Users describe light pressing or rubbing around the orbital rim in short daily sessions, sometimes alongside mewing and other bonehack routines, and judge results from eye-area photos over months.

Medical sources associate vigorous eye rubbing with progression of keratoconus, a corneal condition, and the orbit surrounds the eye and optic structures. Pressure near the eye has not been studied as a cosmetic technique.

angle.text: Orbital rubbing is used in the hope of a more open, defined eye area by pressing around the eye socket. No study has tested whether massage changes the orbital bones, and the practice is documented mainly in forum posts.

lead: Orbital rubbing, also called eye socket massage, is a bonehacking practice in which a person presses or rubs the area around the eye socket in the belief that it can change the shape or position of the orbit and so the look of the eyes. Its goal is usually the so-called hunter eyes look, which the Wikipedia looksmaxxing article describes as a positive canthal tilt with little or no upper eyelid showing and low-set eyebrows.[1]

Wikipedia notes that some people try to reach that look through mewing, rubbing the orbital area or surgery.[1] Practitioners see the eye area as a high-impact facial feature and orbital rubbing as a free, non-surgical route to a more intense, narrower or more upturned eye appearance.

The bony orbit is a cavity formed by seven bones that protects the eye.[2] No published clinical study located has tested whether manual pressure or massage can remodel the adult orbital bones. Separately, medical literature associates vigorous rubbing of the eye itself with progression of the corneal condition keratoconus.[3]
infobox: Hunter eyes (positive canthal tilt, little upper lid show) [1]

paras: The practice is framed by its proponents as applying manual pressure around the orbital rim or eye socket to alter eye shape. The anatomy involved is a pyramid-shaped cavity opening at the face and tapering toward the back of the skull, whose walls are made of seven bones of different embryological origin [2]. The thin inner wall formed by the ethmoid bone is described as easily fractured in trauma, and the lateral wall as the thickest [2].

The practice appears in looksmaxxing and bonehacking discussion alongside mewing and other non-surgical methods the Wikipedia looksmaxxing article groups under softmaxxing, though the article does not describe orbital rubbing in detail.[1] Community material on orbital rubbing specifically is sparse, and no named originator was located.

No studies found. Medical literature on eye rubbing concerns the cornea rather than the orbital bones: several observational reports and case series cited in the keratoconus literature link frequent or vigorous eye rubbing with onset or progression of the condition, and clinicians commonly advise patients to avoid the habit [3].

Because the practice involves pressure near the eye, ophthalmology sources on eye rubbing are the closest relevant evidence. Reports associate repeated, forceful rubbing with keratoconus, a condition in which the cornea thins and bulges [3]. Orbital anatomy sources also note that conditions affecting orbital contents can lead to loss of vision if untreated [2]. These sources do not address massage around the socket as a technique.

The Wikipedia looksmaxxing article reports that doctors have called related practices such as mewing and bonesmashing misinformation and that facial surgeons warn of risks including vision changes from forceful facial trauma; it does not address orbital rubbing as a separate technique.[1] Ophthalmology literature recommends discouraging habitual vigorous eye rubbing because of keratoconus progression.[3]
